pos: n. (Casiodoro de Reina, c. 1520–1594, monk of San Isidoro who made the first complete Spanish Bible from the original tongues)
etymology: Spanish Casiodoro, from Latin Cassiodorus; de Reina, of Reina, a town in Extremadura.
biblical_def: Casiodoro de Reina was a monk of the Hieronymite house of San Isidoro del Campo outside Seville, where a copy of Juan Pérez's New Testament and a reading of the Reformers turned the whole community. When the Holy Office closed on them in 1557 some twelve of the brethren fled; Reina reached Geneva, then London, where Elizabeth gave the Spanish refugees a church, then Antwerp, Frankfurt and Basel, hunted by Spanish agents the whole way and condemned in effigy at Seville. For twelve years he worked at the Scriptures, using the Hebrew and Greek with Pérez's version and the Ferrara Jewish Bible before him, and in 1569 printed at Basel the first complete Spanish Bible made from the originals. Its title-page device of a bear reaching into a honey-tree gave it the name it still carries, the Bible of the Bear. He spent his last years as a Lutheran pastor to the Frankfurt exiles and died there. One man, hunted across four countries, gave a nation its Bible. “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation, and void as empty, vain, having no effect.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; the act of translating, or the work translated.
VOID, a. Empty; vacant; not occupied; having no legal or binding force; vain.
HI'ERONYMITE, n. One of a religious order under the patronage of St Jerome.
FU'GITIVE, n. One who flees from his station or duty; one who flees from danger.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
corruption_summary: The hunted monk of San Isidoro who gave Spain the Bible of the Bear.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a sectarian one. Reina is claimed by Lutherans for his Frankfurt pastorate and suspected by some Reformed writers for the same reason, and both parties use the question of his later affiliation to avoid the work he actually did. He translated the Bible into Spanish; that is the fact that bears on the church.

The principle to recover is that the word is not at the mercy of the men who carry it, and that a translator's chains do not bind the text. Paul writes from prison with the distinction exactly drawn: “Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). Seville burned Reina in effigy and could not burn the Bible of the Bear.

pos: n. (Cipriano de Valera, c. 1532–c. 1602, monk of San Isidoro, reviser of the Spanish Bible and translator of Calvin's Institutes)
etymology: Spanish Cipriano, from Latin Cyprianus, of Cyprus; de Valera, of Valera in Extremadura.
biblical_def: Cipriano de Valera fled San Isidoro del Campo with Reina and the rest of the brethren in 1557 and spent the remaining forty-five years of his life in England, first at Cambridge and Oxford, where he took degrees and taught, then in London among the Spanish exiles. He wrote against the papacy and the mass for Spanish readers who would have to receive the books by smuggling, and in 1597 he put Calvin's Institutes into Spanish — the one work that could set a whole system before a reader cut off from every Protestant pulpit. In 1602, after twenty years at the task, he published at Amsterdam his revision of Reina's Bible, correcting, re-ordering the apocryphal books into an appendix, and smoothing the Spanish. That revision, not the first edition, became the Bible of the Spanish-speaking world; the version has borne both their names ever since. He is the type of a reviser, a man content to spend two decades improving another's work. “But the word of the Lord endureth for ever” (1Pe 1:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revision as the act of reviewing for correction, and an institute as a system of elements or rules.
webster_full: REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.
IN'STITUTE, n. Established law; settled order; a book of elements or principles.
APOC'RYPHA, n. Books whose authors are not known; books not admitted as inspired.
ENDURE', v. To last; to continue in the same state; to remain; to abide.
scriptures: But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
corruption_summary: The exile who spent twenty years revising another man's Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern appetite for the original and the authentic: a reviser is treated as a lesser figure than a translator, and Valera's twenty years are mentioned as a footnote to Reina's twelve. The Spanish church has read Valera's text for four centuries, which settles whose labour reached the people.

The principle to recover is that the labour of correction is a ministry and not a vanity, because the thing corrected is a word that must be exact to be useful: “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Pro 30:5). A man who spends his life making a translation purer has spent it on the shield itself, and Jeremiah names what he is handling: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29).

pos: n. (the Spanish Bible of Casiodoro de Reina, 1569, as revised by Cipriano de Valera, 1602)
etymology: Named for its translator and its reviser; known from its first title-page device as la Biblia del Oso, the Bible of the Bear.
biblical_def: The Reina-Valera is to Spanish what the Authorized Version is to English: the translation that formed a language's religious speech and held the field for centuries. Casiodoro de Reina printed the first complete Spanish Bible from the Hebrew and Greek at Basel in 1569, about twenty-six hundred copies, with a woodcut of a bear at a honey-tree on the title page. Cipriano de Valera revised it over twenty years and published the result at Amsterdam in 1602, and that text, further revised in 1862, 1909, 1960 and since, is the Bible of Spanish-speaking Protestantism. Every copy of the first editions had to be smuggled into Spain, where possession was a matter for the Holy Office, and the version did its first work among exiles and prisoners. Its history is the plainest refutation of the claim that the Spanish-speaking peoples had no Protestant Scriptures until modern missions arrived: they had them in 1569, and the men who made them died hunted or in exile. “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to publish as to make known to mankind or to people in general, and a copy as a transcript or an individual book of an impression.
webster_full: PUB'LISH, v. To discover or make known to mankind or to people in general; to proclaim; to utter.
COP'Y, n. A transcript; an imitation or resemblance; a single book or set of an impression.
SMUG'GLE, v. To import or export secretly goods which are forbidden by law.
IMPRES'SION, n. The whole number of copies printed at one time; an edition.
scriptures: The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
Col 4:16
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.
Rev 1:3
Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand.
Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them.
corruption_summary: The Bible of the Bear, smuggled into a country that forbade it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern treatment of the Reina-Valera is usually a quarrel over which revision is the true one, carried on with the same heat as the English version controversies and often by the same argument: that a particular printing is the providentially preserved text and every later correction is corruption. The dictionary does not take that ground for any language. A translation is a human work serving a divine text, and the proper question of any revision is whether it renders the Hebrew and Greek more faithfully.

The principle to recover is that Scripture is given to be read aloud in the churches and passed from congregation to congregation, which is why a version in the people's tongue is not a convenience but an obedience. Paul gives the instruction as a command: “And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans” (Col 4:16). The blessing attaches to the reading and the hearing: “Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy” (Rev 1:3).

pos: n. (Francisco de Enzinas, 1518–1552, of Burgos, first translator of the New Testament into Spanish)
etymology: Spanish Francisco, the Frenchman; Enzinas, of the oak-groves, from encina, the holm-oak; latinised Dryander.
biblical_def: Francisco de Enzinas was a merchant's son of Burgos who studied at Louvain and then at Wittenberg, where he lodged in Melanchthon's house and was given the Spanish name of a Greek oak. There he finished a Spanish New Testament from the Greek, printed it at Antwerp in 1543, and did what no one else attempted: he carried it in person to Charles V at Brussels and asked the emperor's leave to circulate it. Charles passed the book to his confessor, and Enzinas was in prison within a fortnight. He lay fifteen months in the Vrunte at Brussels, wrote an account of the Spanish persecutions that is a primary source to this day, and in February 1545 walked out through a door left unlocked. He was made professor of Greek at Cambridge under Edward VI, returned to Strasbourg, and died of the plague at thirty-four. His brother Jaime was burned at Rome. “What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops” (Mat 10:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines boldness as courage, or freedom from timidity in speaking, and a dedication as an address prefixed to a book.
webster_full: BOLD'NESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; freedom from timidity in speaking or writing.
DEDICA'TION, n. An address to a patron, prefixed to a book, testifying respect.
PRISON, n. A house for the confinement of criminals or debtors; a jail.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house; in the East, a flat roof used as a place of resort.

Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: The man who handed his Spanish New Testament to the emperor and went to prison for it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Where Enzinas is noticed he is usually read as naive — a young scholar who did not understand the world he was walking into when he presented a vernacular Testament to Charles V. The Memoirs he wrote in the Brussels prison show a man who understood it precisely and had decided that the book should be asked for openly rather than smuggled, so that the refusal would be on the record.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is not a private possession to be whispered, and that the apostolic prayer under threat was not for safety but for speech: “And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word” (Act 4:29). The angel's order to the released apostles was to go back to the most public place in the city: “Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (Act 5:20).

pos: n. (Juan Pérez de Pineda, c. 1500–1566, Sevillian exile at Geneva, translator of the Spanish New Testament and Psalms)
etymology: Spanish Juan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Pérez, son of Pedro; de Pineda, of the pine-wood.
biblical_def: Juan Pérez de Pineda had been rector of the College of Doctrine at Seville and an imperial agent at Rome before the Holy Office began to move against the Sevillian evangelicals; he escaped to Geneva about 1555 and became the minister of the Spanish congregation there. From Geneva he printed what the men at home needed most: a Spanish New Testament in 1556, the Psalms in 1557, a catechism, and a Spanish version of Juan de Valdés on Romans and First Corinthians. The books went into Spain in casks and bales by the hands of Julián Hernández, and they were the immediate occasion of the Seville and Valladolid prosecutions. He died at Paris in 1566 and left his estate for the printing of a Spanish Bible — the legacy that helped carry Casiodoro de Reina's work to the press at Basel three years later. Few men have left a will that bore fruit so exactly. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and a legacy as a bequest, a particular thing given by last will.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; sometimes applied to a psalm-book.
LEG'ACY, n. A bequest; a particular thing, or certain sum of money, given by last will.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
SIM'PLE, a. Artless; unaffected; undesigning; sincere; weak in intellect; not wise.
scriptures: Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
corruption_summary: The Geneva printer-pastor whose will paid for the Bible of the Bear.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suggestion, made by both devout and sceptical writers, that the Geneva exiles provoked the Spanish persecutions and so bear some blame for the deaths at Seville. The reasoning would make every printer of Scripture responsible for the tribunal that burns its readers, and it reverses the plain moral order of the thing.

The principle to recover is that the Psalter is the church's own book of praise and complaint, and that a persecuted people needs it in its own tongue before it needs anything else but the Gospels. Pérez printed the Psalms second for that reason. “But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) is not a counsel for scholars; it is the daily food of a man whose Bible has to be hidden in a wine cask.

pos: n. (Constantino Ponce de la Fuente, c. 1502–1560, canon and preacher of Seville cathedral, chaplain to Charles V)
etymology: Spanish Constantino, from Latin Constantinus, steadfast; Ponce de la Fuente, of the fountain.
biblical_def: Constantino Ponce de la Fuente was the most celebrated preacher in Spain. Canon-magistral of Seville cathedral, doctor of theology, author of catechisms and expositions that sold in editions, he was taken by Charles V as his own chaplain and preached before the emperor in the Low Countries and at his retirement. He used the cathedral pulpit of Seville for twenty years to preach the free justification of sinners in language careful enough to pass and plain enough to be understood, and a congregation grew around it that the Holy Office at last uncovered through the papers of a dead colleague. He was arrested in August 1558, confronted with his own concealed manuscripts, and held in the Triana castle, where he died in 1560 before sentence; his bones and his effigy were burned at the auto-de-fe of 22 December that year, with his books. He is the dictionary's Spanish case of a man preaching the gospel inside an institution that would kill him for it. “woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!” (1Co 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a dignitary of a cathedral church, and a pulpit as an elevated place in which a preacher stands.
webster_full: CAN'ON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend in a cathedral.
PUL'PIT, n. An elevated place or inclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands.
EF'FIGY, n. The image or likeness of a person; to burn in effigy, to burn an image of a person.
NECES'SITY, n. That which makes an act or event unavoidable; compulsion.

But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
corruption_summary: Spain's greatest preacher, who died in the Triana and was burned in effigy.
corruption_paragraphs: Constantino is regularly used to argue that the Spanish evangelicals were never Protestants at all but reforming Catholics whom a paranoid Inquisition destroyed needlessly, since he never left the cathedral and died a canon of it. The concealed manuscripts found in his lodging settle the question: they state justification by faith alone, deny purgatory and the sacrifice of the mass, and he had kept them hidden for exactly that reason. A man does not hide what his church permits him to say.

The principle to recover is the weight of the preaching office, which is a necessity laid on a man and not a career he adorns: “For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me” (1Co 9:16). Ezekiel names the alternative, which is the besetting sin of a preacher with a great reputation and a comfortable prebend: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!” (Eze 34:2).

pos: n. (Juan Gil, called Doctor Egidio, d. 1555, canon-magistral of Seville who recanted and was burned after death)
etymology: Spanish Juan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Gil, from Aegidius, latinised Egidio.
biblical_def: Juan Gil, known everywhere as Doctor Egidio, was a learned Aragonese appointed canon-magistral and preacher of Seville cathedral about 1537. He preached without power until Rodrigo de Valer, a layman under penance, told him he was preaching the schoolmen and not the Scriptures; from that rebuke he turned to the Bible, and the cathedral filled. Charles V nominated him bishop of Tortosa in 1549. The Holy Office arrested him in 1550, and after two years of examination he was brought to the cathedral in 1552 to read a recantation in the pulpit where he had preached, and was sentenced to a year's imprisonment and ten years of silence. He was released, visited the brethren in Valladolid, and died in 1555. In the auto of 22 December 1560 his bones were dug up and burned. The dictionary records him with both halves of the record: the man who was turned to the Scriptures by a layman's rebuke, and the man who fell in the pulpit. “And he went out, and wept bitterly” (Mat 26:75) is the pattern the sources suggest and do not prove.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract a declaration or proposition, and restoration as the act of replacing in a former state.
webster_full: RECANT', v. To retract a declaration or proposition; to unsay; to contradict a former declaration.
RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; recovery.
REBUKE', n. A direct and reproachful address; reprehension; chiding.
MAG'ISTRAL, a. Belonging to a master; in Spain, the canon charged with preaching.

corruption_summary: The Seville preacher turned by a layman's rebuke, who afterwards recanted in his own pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: Egidio is handled in two bad ways. Roman accounts treat the recantation as a return to the Church and the later burning of his bones as mere posthumous formality, which ignores that he resumed fellowship with the Valladolid brethren as soon as he was free. Protestant accounts have sometimes suppressed the recantation altogether. The dictionary prints both because the gospel is not served by a cleaned-up martyrology, and because a man who falls and is restored is the commoner Christian experience.

The principle to recover is the Lord's own provision for a servant who is going to fail, which was made before the failure and aimed past it: “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luk 22:32). The prophet states the manner of the Messiah's dealing with such men: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench” (Isa 42:3).

pos: n. (Julián Hernández, d. 1560, called Julianillo, the muleteer who smuggled the Spanish Scriptures into Seville)
etymology: Spanish Julián, from Latin Julianus; Hernández, son of Hernando; the diminutive Julianillo for his small stature.
biblical_def: Julián Hernández was a small, deformed man of Villaverde who had been a servant and a muleteer and who worked in Geneva as a printer's hand for the Spanish exiles. He volunteered to carry their books home. In 1557 he brought two great casks, packed as Rhenish wine and as merchandise, from Geneva through France and over the Pyrenees into Seville, with Juan Pérez's New Testaments and tracts inside, and distributed them to the brethren in the city and to the monks of San Isidoro del Campo. A copy left with the wrong man betrayed the whole network. He was taken, and for nearly three years the Holy Office worked on him with the rack and with promises to make him name the receivers; the record says he gave them nothing of consequence. He was burned at the auto-de-fe of 22 December 1560. The Reformation in Spain was carried in on a crippled muleteer's back and ended in a fire he was tied to. “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1Co 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a muleteer as a mule-driver, and to confound as to perplex, to abash, to put to shame.
webster_full: MULETEE'R, n. A mule-driver; one who drives mules.
CONFOUND', v. To perplex; to abash; to throw into disorder; to put to shame.
CASK, n. A close vessel for containing liquors, formed of staves, heading and hoops.
RACK, n. An engine of torture; the instrument on which criminals are extended to extort confession.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
corruption_summary: Julianillo the muleteer, who brought Spain its Testaments in a wine cask.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the ordinary snobbery of history-writing: the Spanish Reformation is told through the canons and the doctors of Seville, with the man who actually moved the books across the Pyrenees mentioned as a courier. Without the courier there was no Spanish Reformation to write about.

The principle to recover is that God's choice of instruments is deliberately humbling, and that the obscurity of the servant is part of the design rather than an accident of it: “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27). Paul states the reason in the next letter: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7).

pos: n. (Antonio del Corro, 1527–1591, monk of San Isidoro, pastor to the Spanish exiles and reader in divinity at Oxford)
etymology: Spanish Antonio, from the Roman gens Antonius; del Corro, a Sevillian family name.
biblical_def: Antonio del Corro was one of the monks of San Isidoro del Campo who fled in 1557. He studied at Lausanne and Geneva, served French congregations in Béarn and at Antwerp through the troubles of 1566, and came to London, where he was appointed to the Spanish congregation and licensed to preach. There he fell into a long and bitter quarrel with the French and Dutch stranger churches, who required him to subscribe their confession article by article and suspected his orthodoxy on predestination and on the Trinity; he answered that he would subscribe the Scriptures and the Apostles' Creed and thought a confession a fence rather than a foundation. The dispute cost him his pulpit. He ended as reader in divinity at the Temple and at Oxford, where he was given a degree and taught until his death. The dictionary honours the confessor who got out of Seville and names the error plainly: a man who will not be bound by the church's confession has set his own judgment above the brethren's. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to subscribe as to attest by writing one's name, and a confession as a formulary of articles of faith.
webster_full: SUBSCRI'BE, v. To attest by writing one's name beneath; to assent to; to promise by writing.
CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to.
U'NITY, n. The state of being one; concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
FORM, n. A model to be imitated; a prescribed mode or order; a pattern.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: The Sevillian exile who would subscribe the Creed but not the brethren's confession.
corruption_paragraphs: Del Corro is now the favourite of writers who want an irenic, undogmatic sixteenth century: a man persecuted first by the Inquisition and then by the Calvinists for the same crime of thinking freely. The parallel is false and the dictionary refuses it. Seville had him condemned to the fire; London asked him to sign the confession his congregation already held and let him go on teaching when he would not. The one is persecution and the other is the ordinary discipline without which no church can know what it believes.

The principle to recover is that confessional subscription is the servant of unity, not its enemy, because unity is agreement in a stated faith and not politeness about an unstated one. Paul asks for the first: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10). Jude requires the faith to be a definite deposit that can be contended for: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

pos: n. pl. (the Protestants of Seville condemned in the autos-de-fe of 1559 and 1560)
etymology: Seville, from Arabic Ishbiliyah, from Latin Hispalis; martyr, from Greek martus, a witness.
biblical_def: The Seville martyrs were the congregation that the Holy Office destroyed in two great spectacles. By 1557 the gospel was held in the cathedral chapter, in the Hieronymite house of San Isidoro del Campo, in the convent of Santa Paula, and among merchants and gentry of the city, perhaps eight hundred persons in all; the books smuggled by Julián Hernández betrayed the whole. At the auto-de-fe of 24 September 1559 twenty-one were burned, among them María de Bohorques, a girl of twenty-one who answered the theologians from the Scriptures to the last, and Juan Ponce de León of the house of Arcos. At the auto of 22 December 1560 fourteen more went to the fire, Julián Hernández among them, with the bones of Doctor Egidio and the effigy of Constantino. Twelve of the San Isidoro brethren had escaped in time, and from them came the Spanish Bible. After Seville there was no organised Protestant congregation in Spain for three hundred years. “These are they which came out of great tribulation” (Rev 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an auto-da-fe as a solemn day held by the Inquisition for the punishment of heretics, and martyrdom as the death of a martyr.
webster_full: AUTO DA FE, n. In Catholic countries, a solemn day held by the Inquisition for the punishment of heretics.
MAR'TYRDOM, n. The death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith.
TRIBULA'TION, n. Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations.
CON'GREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
scriptures: Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
corruption_summary: The autos-de-fe of 1559 and 1560, and the end of the Spanish Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: A standing modern claim is that the numbers burned by the Spanish Inquisition have been inflated by Protestant polemic, and that the tribunal was by the standards of its age a careful court. The Seville records allow the correction and do not blunt the point. The precise count is known because the Holy Office kept it, and the significance is not the total but the completeness: a living church of several hundred in Spain's richest city was identified, tried and annihilated, and the country was closed for three centuries.

The principle to recover is that the roll of the faithful in Hebrews was never closed and that the sixteenth century wrote its own names into it. The catalogue there covers exactly what Seville did — “And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36) — and the psalm the church has always sung over such deaths is the one Paul quotes of himself: “Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22).
